Vanilla RNNs fail to remember things from far back in a sequence — the vanishing gradient kills long-range memory. LSTM was designed in 1997 by Hochreiter & Schmidhuber specifically to fix this.
"What if the network could explicitly learn what to remember, what to forget, and what to output at each step?"
LSTM does this with gates — learnable switches that control the flow of information. Think of it like a smart notepad:
You can write new notes onto it
You can erase old notes you no longer need
You can read from it selectively when producing output
Unlike vanilla RNN which has only one hidden state hₜ, LSTM has two:

The cell state is the real innovation. It runs straight through the sequence with only minor, controlled modifications — allowing gradients to flow freely across hundreds of time steps without vanishing.

c₀ ──────────────────────────────────────► cₜ   (long-term memory highway)
         ↑ forget  ↑ add new info
h₀ ──► [LSTM] ──► [LSTM] ──► [LSTM] ──► hₜ   (short-term, output)
         ↑x₁        ↑x₂        ↑x₃
"How much of the old cell state should I keep?"
Takes previous hidden state hₜ₋₁ and current input xₜ
Passes through sigmoid → output between 0 and 1
Applied element-wise to the old cell state cₜ₋₁
Example: Reading "The cat, which was fluffy, was hungry." When you hit "was", the forget gate discards the subject "cat" stored earlier and prepares for a new subject.
"What new information should I write into cell state?"

iₜ = σ(Wi · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bi)      # How much to write (0-1)
c̃ₜ = tanh(Wc · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bc)  # What to write (-1 to 1)
iₜ decides how much of the candidate to add (sigmoid → 0 to 1)
c̃ₜ is the candidate new memory (tanh → -1 to 1)
Together they form the update to cell state
Example: In a sentiment task, when the network reads "amazing", the input gate writes a strongly positive signal into cell state.
"Combine forget and input to get new long-term memory"
fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ = old memory, selectively erased
iₜ ⊙ c̃ₜ = new information, selectively written
This is the heart of LSTM. The cell state is updated additively — this is what allows gradients to flow without vanishing.
"What part of the cell state should I expose as output?"

oₜ = σ(Wo · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bo)    # What to expose (0-1)
hₜ = oₜ ⊙ tanh(cₜ)              # Filtered cell state = new hidden state
oₜ decides which parts of cell state to reveal
tanh(cₜ) squashes cell state to -1 to 1
hₜ is both the output and what gets passed to the next time step
Example: When predicting the next word after "The sky is", the output gate exposes the "colour/weather context" stored in cell state to help predict "blue" or "cloudy".

fₜ = σ(Wf · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bf)         ← Forget gate
iₜ = σ(Wi · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bi)         ← Input gate
c̃ₜ = tanh(Wc · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bc)     ← Candidate memory
cₜ = fₜ ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + iₜ ⊙ c̃ₜ            ← Cell state update
oₜ = σ(Wo · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bo)         ← Output gate
hₜ = oₜ ⊙ tanh(cₜ)                    ← New hidden state
All four weight matrices Wf, Wi, Wc, Wo are learned during training via backpropagation through time (BPTT).
For an LSTM with input size n and hidden size h:

Each gate has: (n + h) × h weights + h biases

4 gates total:
Parameters = 4 × [(n + h) × h + h]
           = 4 × [h(n + h) + h]
GRU was introduced in 2014 by Cho et al. as a simpler alternative to LSTM. The designers asked:
"Do we really need two separate memory streams (cell state + hidden state) and three gates? Can we achieve the same thing more efficiently?"
The answer was yes — GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into one, and reduces three gates down to two. The result is a lighter, faster model that performs comparably to LSTM on most tasks.
LSTM = a sophisticated notepad with separate long/short term sections and 3 control switches
GRU = a simpler notepad with just 2 control switches, but equally smart
📦 GRU vs LSTM — The Key Structural Difference

LSTM has:                          GRU has:
─────────────────────────          ─────────────────────
✦ Cell state  cₜ  (long term)      ✦ Only hidden state hₜ
✦ Hidden state hₜ (short term)       (serves both purposes)

✦ Forget gate  fₜ                  ✦ Reset gate  rₜ
✦ Input gate   iₜ                  ✦ Update gate zₜ
✦ Output gate  oₜ                  ✦ (no output gate)

✦ 4 weight matrices                ✦ 3 weight matrices
✦ More parameters                  ✦ Fewer parameters
✦ Slower                           ✦ Faster
"How much of the PAST hidden state should I use when computing new candidate memory?"
1 = use all of past hidden state

rₜ = [0.1, 0.9, 0.4, ...]

0.1 → almost ignore past for this slot  (reset)
0.9 → use almost all of past for this slot
0.4 → use 40% of past for this slot

When does reset gate close (→ 0)?
When the current input is so different from the past that old context is irrelevant. For example, starting a new topic mid-paragraph.
"How much should I UPDATE my hidden state vs keep the old one?"
This single gate does the job of both the forget gate AND input gate in LSTM:
zₜ → 1 = take mostly new information (big update)
zₜ → 0 = keep mostly old hidden state (little update)

zₜ = [0.8, 0.2, 0.6, ...]

0.8 → update this slot heavily with new info
0.2 → keep 80% of old hidden state in this slot
0.6 → balanced mix of old and new
h̃ₜ = tanh( Wh · [rₜ ⊙ hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bh )
"Compute what the new hidden state COULD be, using the reset-filtered past and current input"
Notice rₜ ⊙ hₜ₋₁ — the reset gate is applied to the past hidden state before computing candidate. This is what makes the reset gate powerful:

rₜ = 0   →   rₜ ⊙ hₜ₋₁ = 0   →  past is ignored  →  fresh candidate
rₜ = 1   →   rₜ ⊙ hₜ₋₁ = hₜ₋₁ →  full past used   →  context-aware candidate
"New hidden state = weighted blend of old hidden state and new candidate"

(1 - zₜ) ⊙ hₜ₋₁   →  How much OLD state to carry forward
zₜ ⊙ h̃ₜ           →  How much NEW candidate to add
       +            →  Blend them together

zₜ          = [0.8,  0.2,  0.6]   ← update gate
1 - zₜ      = [0.2,  0.8,  0.4]   ← complement

hₜ₋₁        = [0.5,  0.3,  0.7]   ← old hidden state
h̃ₜ         = [0.9, -0.1,  0.4]   ← candidate

(1-zₜ)⊙hₜ₋₁ = [0.10, 0.24, 0.28]  ← old contribution
zₜ ⊙ h̃ₜ    = [0.72,-0.02, 0.24]  ← new contribution

hₜ          = [0.82, 0.22, 0.52]  ← final hidden state ✅

rₜ = σ( Wr · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + br )          ← Reset gate
zₜ = σ( Wz · [hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bz )          ← Update gate
h̃ₜ = tanh( Wh · [rₜ ⊙ hₜ₋₁, xₜ] + bh ) ← Candidate hidden state
hₜ = (1 - zₜ) ⊙ hₜ₋₁ + zₜ ⊙ h̃ₜ        ← Final hidden state
Just 4 equations vs LSTM's 6. Cleaner, faster, equally powerful.
For input size n and hidden size h:

GRU:
  3 weight matrices (reset, update, candidate)
  Parameters = 3 × [(n + h) × h + h]

LSTM:
  4 weight matrices (forget, input, candidate, output)
  Parameters = 4 × [(n + h) × h + h]
Based on Many to many RNN architecture
Before Seq2Seq, RNNs had a fundamental limitation — input and output had to be the same length. But real tasks don't work that way:

"How are you?"        →  "Bien merci"        (3 words → 2 words)
"Hello"               →  "Bonjour"           (1 word  → 1 word)
"I love machine learning" → "J'aime l'apprentissage automatique" (4 → 3 words)
Seq2Seq, introduced by Sutskever et al. (2014) at Google, solved this with a beautiful idea:
"Split the job into two networks — one that reads and understands the input, and another that generates the output."
Reads the input sequence word by word
Builds up a compressed understanding of the entire input
Produces a single vector called the context vector (also called thought vector)
After reading all input words, it stops — its job is done
Takes the context vector as its starting memory
At each step, feeds its own previous output as the next input
Stops when it generates a special <END> token

ENCODER                          DECODER
──────────────────────           ──────────────────────────────
"How"  → [RNN] → h₁             context → [RNN] → "Bien"
"are"  → [RNN] → h₂             "Bien"  → [RNN] → "merci"
"you?" → [RNN] → h₃ ──► 🔵 ──► "merci" → [RNN] → <END>
                    context
                    vector
⚙️ How It Works — Step by Step

Input: "How are you?"

Step 1: Embed "How"  → x₁ → Encoder RNN → h₁
Step 2: Embed "are"  → x₂ → Encoder RNN → h₂  (uses h₁)
Step 3: Embed "you?" → x₃ → Encoder RNN → h₃  (uses h₂)

Final hidden state h₃ = Context Vector 🔵
The context vector is supposed to capture the entire meaning of "How are you?" in a fixed-size vector (e.g., 256 numbers).

Start with: context vector + special <START> token

Step 1: <START> + context → Decoder RNN → predicts "Bien"
Step 2: "Bien"  + hd₁    → Decoder RNN → predicts "merci"
Step 3: "merci" + hd₂    → Decoder RNN → predicts <END>
                                                      ↑
                                               Stop generating

At each step t:
  hₜ, cₜ = LSTM(xₜ, hₜ₋₁, cₜ₋₁)

Final output:
  context = (h_final, c_final)   ← both hidden & cell state passed to decoder

Initialise with:
  hd₀ = h_final  (encoder's final hidden state)
  cd₀ = c_final  (encoder's final cell state)

At each step t:
  hd_t, cd_t = LSTM(yₜ₋₁, hd_{t-1}, cd_{t-1})
  output_t   = softmax(W · hd_t)    ← probability over vocab
  yₜ         = argmax(output_t)     ← pick most likely word
🎯 Training vs Inference — A Critical Difference
The decoder is given the real previous word, not its own prediction:

Target: "Bien merci <END>"

Step 1: Feed <START>  → predict "Bien"  ✅ (correct: "Bien")
Step 2: Feed "Bien"   → predict "merci" ✅ (correct: "merci")  ← real word, not prediction
Step 3: Feed "merci"  → predict <END>   ✅
This speeds up training dramatically — errors don't compound.
The decoder uses its own predictions as input:

Step 1: Feed <START>  → predict "Bien"
Step 2: Feed "Bien"   → predict "merci"   ← own prediction fed back
Step 3: Feed "merci"  → predict <END>
Here's the critical weakness of vanilla Seq2Seq:

"The cat sat on the mat and looked at the dog"
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
              10 words of meaning
                      ↓
               [  256 numbers  ]   ← context vector
                      ↓
        "Le chat était assis sur le tapis
         et regardait le chien"
One fixed-size vector must carry ALL the meaning of the input. For long sentences this becomes a severe bottleneck — early words get "forgotten" by the time the encoder finishes.
This is what motivated the invention of Attention — but that's a separate topic!

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import random

# ── 1. Encoder ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim, hidden_size,
                 num_layers=2, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, padding_idx=0)
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(
            embed_dim, hidden_size,
            num_layers=num_layers,
            batch_first=True,
            dropout=dropout
        )
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (batch, src_seq_len)
        embedded = self.dropout(self.embedding(x))
        # embedded: (batch, src_seq_len, embed_dim)

        outputs, (hidden, cell) = self.lstm(embedded)
        # outputs: (batch, src_seq_len, hidden)  ← all hidden states
        # hidden:  (num_layers, batch, hidden)   ← final hidden state
        # cell:    (num_layers, batch, hidden)   ← final cell state

        return hidden, cell   # context vector — passed to decoder

# ── 2. Decoder ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class Decoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim, hidden_size,
                 num_layers=2, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, padding_idx=0)
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(
            embed_dim, hidden_size,
            num_layers=num_layers,
            batch_first=True,
            dropout=dropout
        )
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, vocab_size)
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x, hidden, cell):
        # x: (batch,) — one token at a time
        x = x.unsqueeze(1)   # (batch, 1) — add seq dimension

        embedded = self.dropout(self.embedding(x))
        # embedded: (batch, 1, embed_dim)

        output, (hidden, cell) = self.lstm(embedded, (hidden, cell))
        # output: (batch, 1, hidden)

        prediction = self.fc(output.squeeze(1))
        # prediction: (batch, vocab_size) — scores for each word

        return prediction, hidden, cell

# ── 3. Seq2Seq — Puts It All Together ────────────────────────
class Seq2Seq(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, encoder, decoder, device):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = encoder
        self.decoder = decoder
        self.device  = device

    def forward(self, src, trg, teacher_forcing_ratio=0.5):
        # src: (batch, src_len)
        # trg: (batch, trg_len)
        batch_size = src.shape[0]
        trg_len    = trg.shape[1]
        trg_vocab  = self.decoder.fc.out_features

        # Store all decoder outputs
        outputs = torch.zeros(batch_size, trg_len, trg_vocab).to(self.device)

        # ── Encode ──────────────────────────────────────────
        hidden, cell = self.encoder(src)

        # First decoder input = <START> token (index 1)
        dec_input = trg[:, 0]   # (batch,)

        # ── Decode word by word ──────────────────────────────
        for t in range(1, trg_len):
            prediction, hidden, cell = self.decoder(dec_input, hidden, cell)
            outputs[:, t, :] = prediction

            # Teacher forcing: use real word or model's prediction
            use_teacher = random.random() < teacher_forcing_ratio
            top_word    = prediction.argmax(1)   # model's best guess
            dec_input   = trg[:, t] if use_teacher else top_word

        return outputs   # (batch, trg_len, vocab_size)

# ── 4. Instantiate & Train ───────────────────────────────────
device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')

SRC_VOCAB = 8000
TRG_VOCAB = 10000
EMBED_DIM  = 256
HIDDEN     = 512
LAYERS     = 2

encoder = Encoder(SRC_VOCAB, EMBED_DIM, HIDDEN, LAYERS)
decoder = Decoder(TRG_VOCAB, EMBED_DIM, HIDDEN, LAYERS)
model   = Seq2Seq(encoder, decoder, device).to(device)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=0)  # ignore padding

# Training step
def train_step(src, trg):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    output = model(src, trg, teacher_forcing_ratio=0.5)
    # output: (batch, trg_len, vocab)
    # trg:    (batch, trg_len)

    # Reshape for loss: skip <START> token at position 0
    output = output[:, 1:, :].reshape(-1, TRG_VOCAB)
    trg    = trg[:, 1:].reshape(-1)

    loss = criterion(output, trg)
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    optimizer.step()
    return loss.item()

# Test forward pass
src = torch.randint(1, SRC_VOCAB, (32, 15)).to(device)  # batch=32, src_len=15
trg = torch.randint(1, TRG_VOCAB, (32, 12)).to(device)  # batch=32, trg_len=12
out = model(src, trg)
print(f"Output shape: {out.shape}")  # → (32, 12, 10000)

```
## ✅ Strengths of Seq2Seq

- Handles **variable length** input and output naturally
- Clean separation of **understanding** (encoder) and **generation** (decoder)
- Works for any sequence transformation task
- Foundation for modern NLP architectures

## ❌ Limitations

| Problem | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Bottleneck** | One vector can't capture long sequences well |
| **Sequential** | Can't be parallelized — slow to train |
| **Forgetting** | Early words lost in long sequences |
| **Fixed context** | Decoder can't look back at encoder states |

## 🔮 What Comes Next?

Seq2Seq's bottleneck problem directly motivated two major innovations:
```
Seq2Seq (2014)
     ↓
Seq2Seq + Attention (2015)  ← decoder looks at ALL encoder states

A vanilla RNN forgets things from far back in a sentence. LSTM fixes this by having two separate memory systems — one for short term, one for long term.

Step 1 — Two memories enter the cell
At every word, LSTM receives two things from the previous step:

hₜ₋₁  →  short term memory  "what I just saw"
cₜ₋₁  →  long term memory   "what I've been carrying for a while"
Plus the current word xₜ as input.

Step 2 — Forget Gate decides what to throw away
The cell looks at the current word and short term memory and asks:
"Is anything in my long term memory now useless?"
It produces values between 0 and 1 for each memory slot:

0  →  completely erase this slot
1  →  keep this slot fully
For example, if the sentence changes topic, old context gets erased here.

Step 3 — Input Gate decides what new info to write
Now it asks:
"What new information from the current word is worth saving?"

Input gate   →  HOW MUCH new info to write  (0 to 1)
Candidate    →  WHAT new info to write      (-1 to 1)
These two are multiplied together — only important new info gets written.

Step 4 — Long term memory gets updated
The long term memory cₜ is now updated:

Old memory  ×  forget gate   →  what survived from before
New info    ×  input gate    →  what gets added now
Add both together            →  new long term memory
This is the heart of LSTM — memory is updated additively, which prevents gradients from vanishing.

Step 5 — Output Gate decides what to expose
Not everything in long term memory is relevant right now. The output gate asks:
"Which parts of long term memory should I share as output?"
It filters the long term memory and produces the new short term memory hₜ.
Step 6 — Two outputs leave the cell

hₜ  →  short term memory  passed to next step + used as output
cₜ  →  long term memory   passed to next step silently
This repeats for every word in the sequence.
LSTM has two memory lanes — a long term highway that carries important info across many steps, and a short term output. Three gates control what gets erased, written, and exposed at each step.
LSTM works great but has lots of parameters and two separate memory streams. GRU simplifies this into one memory stream and two gates — faster and nearly as powerful.

Step 1 — Only one memory enters
Unlike LSTM's two inputs, GRU only receives:

hₜ₋₁  →  one single hidden state  "everything I remember"
xₜ    →  current word
No separate long term memory — one stream does both jobs.

Step 2 — Reset Gate decides how much past to use
The reset gate asks:
"When computing new candidate memory, how much of my past should I look at?"

reset → 0  →  ignore the past completely  (fresh start)
reset → 1  →  use all of the past         (full context)
This is applied before computing new candidate memory — it controls how context-aware the new memory will be.

Step 3 — Candidate memory is computed
Using the reset-filtered past and the current word, a candidate new memory is computed:
candidate = tanh( current word + reset gate × past hidden state )
This is what the new hidden state could be — but not necessarily what it will be.

Step 4 — Update Gate decides how much to change
This is GRU's most powerful gate. It asks:
"Should I update my hidden state a lot or a little?"

update → 1  →  replace mostly with new candidate
update → 0  →  keep mostly the old hidden state
Notice — this single gate does the job of both the forget gate AND input gate from LSTM. It's a blend dial between old and new.
Step 5 — New hidden state is a blend

new hidden state = (1 - update) × old hidden state
                 +  update      × candidate
Keep some of the old  +  Add some of the new  =  Updated memory
hₜ  →  the single hidden state, passed to next step and used as output

GRU has one memory stream and two gates — the reset gate controls how much past context to use when forming new memory, and the update gate controls how much the memory actually changes. Simpler than LSTM, nearly as powerful.
Normal RNNs require input and output to be the same length. But translation, summarisation, and chatbots need different length inputs and outputs. Seq2Seq splits the job into two separate networks.

Step 1 — Read the input sentence word by word
The encoder is just an LSTM or GRU that reads the source sentence:

"How"  →  LSTM  →  hidden state h₁
"are"  →  LSTM  →  hidden state h₂
"you?" →  LSTM  →  hidden state h₃
Each step updates the hidden state with new information.

Step 2 — Discard everything except the last hidden state
After reading all words, the encoder throws away all intermediate hidden states and keeps only the final one:
h₃  →  this is called the CONTEXT VECTOR
This single vector is supposed to capture the entire meaning of the input sentence — like compressing a paragraph into a sticky note.

Step 3 — Encoder stops — its job is done
The encoder hands the context vector to the decoder and steps aside.

Step 4 — Decoder starts with the context vector
The decoder initialises its hidden state with the encoder's context vector:
decoder hidden state  =  context vector  "I know what the source means"

Step 5 — Feed a special START token
The decoder is given a special <START> token as its first input — a signal that says:

Step 6 — Predict the first output word
The decoder combines the START token and context vector to predict the first word:
It looks at probabilities over the entire vocabulary and picks the most likely word.

Step 7 — Feed prediction back as next input
The predicted word becomes the input for the next step:
This is called autoregressive generation — the model feeds itself.

Step 8 — Stop at END token
When the decoder generates the special <END> token, it stops. The collected words form the output sentence:
During training, instead of feeding the model's own predictions back, you feed the real correct words:

Step 1: feed <START>  →  predict "Bien"
Step 2: feed "Bien"   →  predict "merci"   ← real word, not model's guess
Step 3: feed "merci"  →  predict <END>
This makes training faster and more stable — errors don't snowball.

Seq2Seq has two networks — the encoder reads and compresses the entire input into one context vector, and the decoder starts from that vector and generates the output word by word until it decides to stop.

LSTM / GRU
  ↓
used as building blocks inside...
  ↓
Seq2Seq  (encoder + decoder, both made of LSTM/GRU)
  ↓
still had a bottleneck — one context vector not enough
  ↓
Attention  (decoder looks at ALL encoder steps, not just the last)
  ↓
Transformer  (attention everywhere, no RNN needed at all)

Step 1 — Read the input sentence word by word
The encoder reads each word one at a time. For example:

"The"  →  processed  →  saves hidden state h₁
"black" → processed  →  saves hidden state h₂
"cat"  →  processed  →  saves hidden state h₃

Step 2 — Keep ALL hidden states, not just the last one
Unlike vanilla Seq2Seq which only kept the final hidden state, attention saves every single hidden state from every word.

h₁ = memory of "The"
h₂ = memory of "black"
h₃ = memory of "cat"
... and so on
Think of these as individual notes the encoder took while reading each word.

Step 3 — Decoder looks at ALL encoder notes
When the decoder wants to generate a word, it first looks at all the encoder's saved hidden states and asks:
"Which of these notes is most useful to me RIGHT NOW?"

Step 4 — Give each encoder note a relevance score
The decoder compares its current state against every encoder hidden state and assigns a score to each:

h₁ ("The")   → score: 0.05   → not very relevant
h₂ ("black") → score: 0.10   → somewhat relevant
h₃ ("cat")   → score: 0.85   → very relevant ✅
Higher score = more relevant to the current decoding step.

Step 5 — Convert scores into weights using Softmax
The raw scores are converted into proper weights that all add up to 1 — like percentages:

h₁ → 5%  attention
h₂ → 10% attention
h₃ → 85% attention   ← focus here
This is called the attention distribution.

Step 6 — Build a dynamic context vector
Now multiply each encoder hidden state by its attention weight and add them all up:
This produces a single vector that is heavily influenced by "cat" — the most relevant word. This context vector is different at every decoding step — that's the magic!

Step 7 — Decoder combines context + its own hidden state
The decoder takes two things together:

Its own hidden state  →  "what I've generated so far"
Context vector        →  "what I should focus on in the source"
These are combined together into one vector.

Step 8 — Predict the next word
That combined vector is passed through a final layer which outputs probabilities over the entire vocabulary:
The word with the highest probability is picked — "chat" (French for cat).

Step 9 — Repeat for every output word
The decoder repeats steps 3 to 8 for every word it generates. Each time, the attention weights shift to focus on different source words:

Generating "Le"    → focus on "The"   (h₁)
Generating "noir"  → focus on "black" (h₂)
Generating "chat"  → focus on "cat"   (h₃)

Step 10 — Stop when <END> token is generated
The decoder keeps generating words until it produces a special end token, which signals it's done.

SOURCE SENTENCE:
"The    black    cat"
  ↓       ↓       ↓
  h₁      h₂      h₃   ← encoder saves ALL hidden states

          ↓  ↓  ↓
       ATTENTION LAYER
    "which note matters most?"
          ↓  ↓  ↓
       5% 10% 85%      ← attention weights

          ↓
    context vector     ← weighted mix, mostly h₃

          ↓
    decoder hidden state + context vector

          ↓
       "chat" ✅        ← predicted French word

The encoder takes individual notes for every word. The decoder, at each step, reads all those notes, decides which ones matter most right now, and uses that focused information to generate the next word.

Creational design patterns are a subset of design patterns in software development. They deal with the process of object creation, trying to make it more flexible and efficient. It makes the system independent and how its objects are created, composed, and represented.

Structural design patterns are a subset of design patterns in software development that focus on the composition of classes or objects to form larger, more complex structures. They help in organizing and managing relationships between objects to achieve greater flexibility, reusability, and maintainability in a software system.

Behavioural design patterns are a subset of design patterns in software development that deal with the communication and interaction between objects and classes. They focus on how objects and classes collaborate and communicate to accomplish tasks and responsibilities.

Here is a sample YAML file (azure-pipelines.yml) that demonstrates how to schedule and run a Python script using a cron trigger.

# azure-pipelines.yml
# This YAML pipeline schedules and runs a Python script.

trigger: none  # Prevents the pipeline from running on every code commit.

pr: none       # Disables pipeline runs on pull requests.

schedules:
- cron: "0 8 * * *"  # A cron expression for running at 8:00 AM every day
  displayName: 'Daily Python Script Execution'
  branches:
    include:
    - main           # The branch on which the schedule will run.
  always: true       # Run the pipeline even if there are no code changes since the last run.

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'  # Use a hosted agent with Ubuntu.

steps:
- task: UsePythonVersion@0
  inputs:
    versionSpec: '3.9'    # Specify the Python version to use.
  displayName: 'Install Python'

- script: |
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    pip install -r requirements.txt  # Install required Python packages.
  displayName: 'Install dependencies'

- script: |
    python your_script.py  # Execute your Python script.
  displayName: 'Run Python script'
trigger and pr: Setting both to none ensures the pipeline won't run automatically on code pushes or pull requests. This is crucial for a scheduled-only job.
schedules: This is the core of the scheduling.

cron: The cron expression "0 8 * * *" schedules the pipeline to run at 8:00 AM every day. The format is minute hour day_of_month month day_of_week. You can use a cron generator to create the exact time you need.
displayName: A descriptive name for the scheduled task.
branches: Specifies the branch on which the schedule should run. This prevents the job from running on all branches.
always: If set to true, the pipeline runs on schedule regardless of whether there have been any new code changes since the last run.
pool: Defines the virtual machine (VM) image for the agent that will run the job. ubuntu-latest is a good choice for most Python projects.
steps: A list of tasks to be executed sequentially.
UsePythonVersion@0: This task installs the specified Python version on the build agent.
pip install: This script block uses pip to install the dependencies listed in your requirements.txt file. Make sure this file is committed to your repository.
python your_script.py: This is the final step where your Python script is executed. Replace your_script.py with the actual name of your script file.
The trigger section determines what events will automatically start your pipeline. This is a fundamental part of continuous integration (CI).
Example: To run the pipeline on every commit to the main branch:YAML
No trigger: You can set trigger: none to disable automatic runs and only allow manual execution.
The pool section specifies the agent (a machine that runs the job) where your pipeline's tasks will be executed.
Example: To use a Microsoft-hosted agent running Ubuntu:YAML
The steps section is the heart of the pipeline, containing the sequence of tasks and scripts that the agent will run.
script: This is a simple command-line script. It's often used for tasks like installing dependencies or running tests.

task: A task is a pre-built, reusable action from the Azure DevOps Marketplace. Tasks are more structured and provide specific functionality, such as installing a Python version or building a Docker image.

steps:
- script: echo 'Hello, World!'
  displayName: 'A simple script'

  inputs:
    versionSpec: '3.9'
  displayName: 'Install Python'

A transformer model is a neural network that learns the context of sequential data and generates new data out of it.
A transformer is a type of artificial intelligence model that learns to understand and generate human-like text by analyzing patterns in large amounts of text data.
is a technique used in natural language processing (NLP) to represent words as vectors of real numbers, so that machines can understand and process human language more effectively.
These vectors are learned from text data, and they capture meaning and relationships.
Raw text consists of characters and words, which are not meaningful to a model. Word embeddings:
Capture semantic meaning (e.g., "good" is close to "great")
Raw text is just a sequence of characters and words, not meaningful to a model. Word embeddings:
Capture semantic meaning (e.g., "good" is close to "great")
Word embeddings capture semantic meaning because words with similar meanings tend to occur in similar contexts, and training adjusts vectors to reflect that.
A word embedding is a 1D vector like (300,), not (1 column with rows).
A sentence embedding is typically a 2D matrix: (num_words, embedding_dim)
It’s a two-part neural network where:
Reads the input sequence (e.g., "I love you")
Encodes it into a fixed-length vector (called the context or hidden state)
Captures the semantic meaning of the input
Takes the encoded context and generates the output sequence
Produces one token at a time (e.g., "Je", then "t'", then "aime")
Instead of processing words one by one (like RNNs), the Transformer processes entire sequences in parallel using a mechanism called self-attention.

Input → Token →│  Encoder    │→ Context Representation

                          ↓
               ┌─────────────┐
              ←│  Decoder    │→ Output Tokens
               └─────────────┘
Since Transformers have no recurrence, they add positional encoding to track the order of tokens

 ↓
Multi-Head Self-Attention  (token attends to all other tokens)

Add & LayerNorm

Add & LayerNorm
Self-Attention helps each word focus on other important words in the input
Multi-Head Attention = multiple attention operations in parallel

Feed Forward

Output Token Prediction
Each token looks at all other tokens and weighs them to decide what's important.

This is essential when you want to compare or retrieve entire documents based on meaning.

Sparse embeddings dominated NLP through techniques like one-hot encoding and TF-IDF vectors. Imagine representing the word “cat” in a vocabulary of 100,000 words: its sparse representation would be a vector of length 100,000 containing all zeros except for a single ’1’ in the position corresponding to “cat”.

Dense embeddings, introduced through models like Word2Vec, revolutionized this approach by mapping words or documents into a much lower-dimensional space (typically 100-1000 dimensions) where every dimension carries meaningful information.
Vector embeddings form the fundamental building blocks of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), serving as the bridge between human language and machine understanding.

Large documents are split into smaller, manageable chunks.
Each chunk is converted into a vector using an embedding model (e.g., OpenAI's text-embedding-ada, Sentence-BERT, etc.).
These vector representations are stored in a vector database (e.g., Pinecone, FAISS, Weaviate) for fast similarity search.
User query is passed through the same embedding model to get a vector.

is a technique used in natural language processing (NLP) to represent words as vectors of real numbers, so that machines can understand and process human language more effectively.

Word embeddings capture semantic meaning because words with similar meanings tend to occur in similar contexts, and training adjusts vectors to reflect that.

It’s a two-part neural network where:
Reads the input sequence (e.g., "I love you")
Encodes it into a fixed-length vector (called the context or hidden state)
Captures the semantic meaning of the input
Takes the encoded context and generates the output sequence
Produces one token at a time (e.g., "Je", then "t'", then "aime")
Instead of processing words one by one (like RNNs), the Transformer processes entire sequences in parallel using a mechanism called self-attention.

A vector is a list (or array) of numbers that represents a piece of data like text, image, audio, or a product, in numerical form.

A vector space is a mathematical environment where vectors (lists of numbers) live and can be compared, measured, or transformed.

this form of data type comes a set of operations that are specifically designed for vector manipulation.
These operations are fundamental to many AI and machine learning tasks, such as recommendation systems, image recognition, and natural language understanding.
Similarity comparison: Seeing if a given vector is similar to a reference vector, in meaning

A common operation for this is called Cosine Similarity - measuring the cosine of the angle between two vectors to determine their similarity. Vectors close in meaning have cosine similarity close to 1 (max is 1 for identical vectors) and those that are far away have low cosine similarity.
Nearest Neighbor Search: Identifying multiple close vectors in the dataset to a given vector.
In vector embedding space we have something called ANN or Approximate Nearest Neighbors,
which gives an approximate result which for genAI applications is sufficient.

Word2Vec is a neural network model developed by Google (2013) that learns to represent individual words as dense vectors in such a way that:
Words with similar meaning are close together in vector space.
Predicts the current word from surrounding context.
Predicts surrounding context words given the current word (often performs better on small data
Doc2Vec (aka Paragraph Vector) is an extension of Word2Vec introduced by Le and Mikolov (2014). It allows you to:
Get a vector representation of an entire document, sentence, or paragraph — not just individual words.
This is essential when you want to compare or retrieve entire documents based on meaning.

Sparse embeddings dominated NLP through techniques like one-hot encoding and TF-IDF vectors. Imagine representing the word “cat” in a vocabulary of 100,000 words: its sparse representation would be a vector of length 100,000 containing all zeros except for a single ’1’ in the position corresponding to “cat”.

Dense embeddings, introduced through models like Word2Vec, revolutionized this approach by mapping words or documents into a much lower-dimensional space (typically 100-1000 dimensions) where every dimension carries meaningful information.
Vector embeddings form the fundamental building blocks of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), serving as the bridge between human language and machine understanding.
Every word, sentence, or token that enters a language model must first be converted into a vector representation that the model can process.
